```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.94, out.width = "100%")
library(manimR)
manim_config(verbosity = "WARNING", progress_bar = FALSE)
# The website shows every scene as a video; installed vignettes and
# R CMD check show the last frame of each scene instead.
in_pkgdown <- identical(Sys.getenv("IN_PKGDOWN"), "true")
knitr::opts_chunk$set(format = if (in_pkgdown) "auto" else "png", quality = "l")
# Renders made outside manim chunks, and LaTeX caches, go to a temporary
# directory instead of the working directory.
manim_config(media_dir = file.path(tempdir(), "manimR-media"))
# Chunks that call LaTeX or ffmpeg run on the website and in development
# checks; elsewhere, as on CRAN, they show their code without its result.
external_ok <- in_pkgdown || identical(Sys.getenv("NOT_CRAN"), "true")
# LaTeX counts only when it compiles a formula: an installation can lack
# the packages of the default template.
has_latex <- external_ok && nzchar(Sys.which("latex")) && nzchar(Sys.which("dvisvgm")) &&
  tryCatch({
    MathTex("x")
    TRUE
  }, error = function(e) FALSE)
```

```{r has-ffmpeg, include = FALSE}
# Chunks that encode video need ffmpeg.
has_ffmpeg <- external_ok && nzchar(Sys.which("ffmpeg"))
```

manimR is a native R port of [Manim Community](https://www.manim.community/),
the animation engine behind many explanatory math videos. You describe a
scene in R code: shapes, text, formulas and graphs, and how they move. manimR
draws every frame and hands the frames to `ffmpeg`, which writes a video, a
GIF or a set of images. There is no Python involved; the drawing is done with
grid on an offscreen ragg device.

The API follows Python manim closely, so the large body of manim examples
and tutorials translates almost line by line. If you already know Python
manim, read [Coming from Python manim](https://adamrsophie.github.io/manimR/articles/coming-from-python.html) next. If you
do not, this vignette is the place to start.

## Installation

Install the package from GitHub:

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("adamrsophie/manimR")
```

manimR itself is pure R, but some features call external programs:

| Program | Needed for | How to get it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ffmpeg` | Video output (MP4, MOV, WebM, GIF) | `brew install ffmpeg`, `sudo apt install ffmpeg`, or <https://ffmpeg.org> |
| LaTeX with `dvisvgm` | `Tex()`, `MathTex()` and everything built on them | `tinytex::install_tinytex()` then `tinytex::tlmgr_install("dvisvgm")`, or a full TeX Live or MiKTeX |
| `typst` | `Typst()` and `MathTypst()` | <https://typst.app>; set `manim_config(typst = "/path/to/typst")` if it is not on the `PATH` |
| Python with Pygments (optional) | Syntax highlighting of any language in `Code()`; without it, a built in highlighter handles R and Python | `pip install pygments` |

Without `ffmpeg` you can still draw mobjects with `plot()` and save single
frames as PNG files. Without LaTeX, `Text()` still works, since it uses
your system fonts.

`manim_check()` reports which of these programs it can find (it is the
counterpart of `manim checkhealth`):

```{r check}
manim_check()
```

## The core ideas

Five ideas cover most of manimR.

* **Mobjects** (mathematical objects) are the things you see: a `Circle()`,
  a `Square()`, a `Text()`, an `Axes()`, a `MathTex()` formula. Most are
  vectorized mobjects (`VMobject`), whose outlines are made of cubic Bezier
  curves. Mobjects can contain other mobjects, and groups such as `VGroup()`
  hold several at once.
* **Scenes** hold the mobjects and run the show. You write a scene as a
  class with a `construct()` method; rendering the scene calls `construct()`.
* **Animations** change mobjects over time: `Create()` draws a shape,
  `Transform()` morphs one shape into another, `FadeIn()` fades in. A scene
  runs them with `self$play()` and pauses with `self$wait()`.
* **The camera** turns the scene into pixels. Its frame is 8 units tall and,
  at the usual 16:9 aspect ratio, about 14.2 units wide, with the origin in
  the middle, x to the right and y up. Positions are in these units, so a
  scene looks the same at every resolution.
* **Rendering** plays the scene from start to finish, captures every frame
  and writes the output file. `render()` does this, with options for the
  resolution, frame rate and file format.

Directions are plain numeric vectors of length 3: `UP` is `c(0, 1, 0)` and
`RIGHT` is `c(1, 0, 0)`, so `2 * UP + RIGHT` is the point (1, 2). The picture
below shows the frame with a `NumberPlane()` grid (one square per unit), the
direction constants, and two points labeled with their coordinates.

```{r coordinates}
plane <- NumberPlane()
arrows <- VGroup(
  Arrow(ORIGIN, 2 * UP, buff = 0, color = YELLOW),
  Arrow(ORIGIN, 2 * RIGHT, buff = 0, color = YELLOW)
)
labels <- VGroup(
  Text("UP", font_size = 28, color = YELLOW)$next_to(arrows[1], UP, buff = 0.1),
  Text("RIGHT", font_size = 28, color = YELLOW)$next_to(arrows[2], RIGHT, buff = 0.1)
)
corner <- function(point, label, direction) {
  VGroup(
    Dot(point, color = RED),
    Text(label, font_size = 22, color = RED)$next_to(point, direction, buff = 0.15)
  )
}
corners <- VGroup(
  corner(c(-6, 3, 0), "(-6, 3)", DR),
  corner(c(6, -3, 0), "(6, -3)", UL)
)
plot(VGroup(plane, arrows, labels, corners))
```

## Your first mobjects

Constructors such as `Circle()` and `Square()` create mobjects. Their
arguments match Python manim's, and RStudio completes them. Methods are
called with `$`, and every method that changes a mobject returns the mobject,
so calls chain:

```{r first-mobjects}
circle <- Circle(radius = 1.5, color = BLUE)$set_fill(BLUE, opacity = 0.3)
square <- Square(side_length = 2, color = YELLOW)$next_to(circle, RIGHT, buff = 0.5)
label <- Text("shapes", font_size = 36)$next_to(VGroup(circle, square), DOWN)
shapes <- VGroup(circle, square, label)$move_to(ORIGIN)
plot(shapes)
```

`plot()` draws a mobject as a single frame on the scene's black background.
It is the fastest way to check a layout: no video is written, and the
picture appears in the RStudio Plots pane. Pass `background_color` to change
the background:

```{r plot-background}
plot(VGroup(circle, label$copy()$set_color(BLACK)), background_color = WHITE)
```

Mobjects are R6 objects, which means they are modified in place:
`square$shift(UP)` moves `square` itself, and `b <- a` does not copy `a`.
Use `$copy()` when you want an independent copy, as above, where the
black label is a copy and the original stays white.

Every mobject stores its outline in `$points`, an n x 3 matrix of Bezier
control points (four rows per cubic curve):

```{r points}
dim(square$points)
square$get_center()
square$width
```

## Your first scene

A scene is an R6 class that inherits from `Scene` and defines a
`construct()` method. Inside `construct()`, `self` is the scene:
`self$play()` runs one or more animations and `self$wait()` holds the
current frame.

```{manim square-to-circle}
SquareToCircle <- R6::R6Class("SquareToCircle", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    circle <- Circle()$set_fill(PINK, opacity = 0.5)
    square <- Square()$rotate(PI / 4)
    self$play(Create(square))
    self$play(Transform(square, circle))
    self$wait(0.5)
  })
)
```

Reading it line by line:

1. `R6::R6Class("SquareToCircle", inherit = Scene, ...)` defines a new scene
   class. The first argument is the class name, which also names the output
   file.
2. `circle` is a pink, half transparent circle, and `square` a square turned
   by 45 degrees. Creating them does not show them yet.
3. `self$play(Create(square))` draws the square's outline and adds it to the
   scene.
4. `self$play(Transform(square, circle))` morphs the square into the circle.
   The mobject on screen is still `square`; it now looks like `circle`.
5. `self$wait(0.5)` holds the last frame for half a second.

Each `play()` lasts one second unless you pass `run_time`, and `wait()`
defaults to one second too.

This vignette shows scenes with a knitr engine (see
[RStudio, knitr, Quarto and Shiny](https://adamrsophie.github.io/manimR/articles/rstudio-knitr-shiny.html)); in a script
you render them yourself, as shown in [Rendering](#rendering) below.

## A shorter way: `manim_scene()`

For quick experiments, `manim_scene()` builds the scene class from a plain
function whose argument is the scene:

```{manim manim-scene}
Shapes <- manim_scene(function(self) {
  shapes <- VGroup(
    Circle(color = BLUE)$set_fill(BLUE, 0.5),
    Square(color = GREEN)$set_fill(GREEN, 0.5),
    Triangle(color = RED)$set_fill(RED, 0.5)
  )$arrange(RIGHT, buff = 1)
  self$play(LaggedStart(lapply(shapes$submobjects, GrowFromCenter), lag_ratio = 0.3))
  self$play(shapes$animate$arrange(DOWN, buff = 0.3)$scale(0.6), run_time = 1.5)
  self$wait(0.5)
}, name = "Shapes")
```

`manim_scene()` also takes a `setup` function, run before `construct`, and a
`base` class such as `MovingCameraScene`. `render()` accepts a bare function
too, which it wraps with `manim_scene()` for you.

## Method chaining and the `$animate` builder

Because methods return the mobject, you can describe a whole layout in one
expression:

```{r chaining}
dots <- VGroup(lapply(1:6, function(i) Dot(radius = 0.12 * i)))
dots$arrange(RIGHT, buff = 0.4)$set_color_by_gradient(BLUE, GREEN, YELLOW)$to_edge(UP)
title <- Text("Six dots", font_size = 40)$next_to(dots, DOWN, buff = 0.6)
plot(VGroup(dots, title))
```

To animate a method call instead of applying it at once, put `$animate`
between the mobject and the method. `square$animate$shift(RIGHT)` is an
animation that moves the square to the right; chain several methods and
they happen together. Arguments for the animation itself, such as
`run_time` or `rate_func`, go in `$animate(...)`:

```{manim animate-builder}
AnimateBuilder <- R6::R6Class("AnimateBuilder", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    square <- Square(color = BLUE)$set_fill(BLUE, 0.4)$shift(4 * LEFT)
    circle <- Circle(color = YELLOW)$shift(3.5 * RIGHT)
    self$add(square, circle)
    self$play(square$animate$shift(3 * RIGHT)$rotate(PI / 4)$set_fill(GREEN, 0.8))
    self$play(
      circle$animate(rate_func = there_and_back)$scale(0.5),
      square$animate$scale(1.5),
      run_time = 1.5
    )
    self$wait(0.5)
  })
)
```

Several animations passed to one `self$play()` run at the same time.
`self$add()` puts mobjects on screen without an animation. Named arguments
of `self$play()`, here `run_time = 1.5`, apply to every animation in the
call.

## A first updater

An updater is a function that runs on every frame. A `ValueTracker` holds a
number you can animate; updaters read it and redraw whatever depends on it.
Here a dot follows a tracker along a number line, and its label is rebuilt
every frame with `always_redraw()`:

```{manim first-updater}
Tracker <- R6::R6Class("Tracker", inherit = Scene,
  public = list(construct = function() {
    line <- NumberLine(x_range = c(-5, 5, 1), length = 10)
    x <- ValueTracker(-4)
    dot <- Dot(color = YELLOW)
    dot$add_updater(function(m) m$move_to(line$number_to_point(x$get_value())))
    label <- always_redraw(function() {
      Text(sprintf("x = %.1f", x$get_value()), font_size = 32)$next_to(dot, UP)
    })
    self$add(line, dot, label)
    self$play(x$animate$set_value(4), run_time = 2)
    self$play(x$animate$set_value(1), run_time = 1)
    self$wait(0.5)
  })
)
```

[Updaters and value trackers](https://adamrsophie.github.io/manimR/articles/updaters.html) covers updaters in depth.

## Text and math

`Text()` renders text with your system fonts. `MathTex()` typesets LaTeX
math, and each string you pass becomes one part you can color or animate
separately:

```{r text-math, eval = has_latex}
words <- Text("Pythagoras", font_size = 48, color = BLUE)
eq <- MathTex("a^2", "+", "b^2", "=", "c^2", font_size = 72)$next_to(words, DOWN, buff = 0.5)
eq[5]$set_color(YELLOW)
plot(VGroup(words, eq))
```

Note that LaTeX backslashes must be doubled in ordinary R strings
(`"\\frac{a}{b}"`), or written in a raw string (`r"(\frac{a}{b})"`).
[Text, math and tables](https://adamrsophie.github.io/manimR/articles/text-and-math.html) has the details.

## Rendering

`render()` plays a scene and writes the output. Give it the scene class (or
a function, or a scene object):

```{r render, eval = has_ffmpeg}
out <- render(SquareToCircle, quality = "l")
basename(out)
str(get_video_metadata(out)[c("width", "height", "avg_frame_rate", "duration")])
```

The main arguments are:

| Argument | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `quality` | `"l"` (854 x 480, 15 fps), `"m"` (1280 x 720, 30 fps), `"h"` (1920 x 1080, 60 fps, the default), `"p"` (2560 x 1440, 60 fps) or `"k"` (3840 x 2160, 60 fps) |
| `format` | `"auto"` (the default: MP4, or MOV when transparent), `"mp4"`, `"mov"`, `"webm"`, `"gif"`, `"png"` (the last frame only) or `"png-sequence"` (every frame as a PNG) |
| `output_file` | The file name; a relative name goes into the video folder (or the image folder for a PNG) |
| `save_last_frame` | `TRUE` is a shorthand for `format = "png"`: save only the final frame |
| `transparent` | Transparent background (MOV, WebM or PNG) |
| `preview` | Open the result when done, in the RStudio Viewer when available |
| `...` | Any other setting of `manim_config()`, such as `background_color` or `frame_rate` |

Without `output_file`, the video goes to
`media/videos/<module>/<quality>/<Scene>.mp4` in the media folder,
where `<quality>` is a folder such as `480p15`. The media folder is in the
session's temporary directory, so nothing is written to your working
directory unless you ask: `manim_config(media_dir = "media")` keeps the
output in a `media` folder there, as Python manim does. Use low quality while you
work and high quality for the final version.

A bare function works as well, which is handy at the console. Such a scene
is called `Scene` unless you name it with `scene_name`:

```{r render-function, eval = has_ffmpeg}
out <- render(function(self) {
  self$play(DrawBorderThenFill(Star(color = GOLD, fill_opacity = 0.8)))
}, quality = "l", format = "gif", scene_name = "Star")
basename(out)
```

For the quickest look at a finished scene, skip the video and save only the
last frame with `format = "png"` (or `save_last_frame = TRUE`, which means
the same). As in Python manim, the default names of GIFs and last frame
images carry the version of the package:

```{r render-last-frame}
png_file <- render(SquareToCircle, quality = "l", format = "png")
basename(png_file)
```

`preview_output()` shows a rendered file in the RStudio Viewer pane, or opens
it with your system's viewer elsewhere. `render(..., preview = TRUE)` calls
it for you:

```{r preview, eval = FALSE}
out <- render(SquareToCircle, quality = "l")
preview_output(out)
```

For scripts that define several scenes, `render_file("scenes.R")` renders
them all, and `manim_cli()` does the same from a terminal, like the `manim`
command. [Rendering, configuration and output](https://adamrsophie.github.io/manimR/articles/rendering.html) covers every
option, the media folder layout, sections, sound and caching.

## A tour of the articles on the website

* [Coming from Python manim](https://adamrsophie.github.io/manimR/articles/coming-from-python.html): a translation guide
  from Python manim code to manimR, with every renamed name and index
  difference.
* [Mobjects and geometry](https://adamrsophie.github.io/manimR/articles/mobjects.html): shapes, lines, arrows, polygons,
  groups, positioning and styling.
* [Animations](https://adamrsophie.github.io/manimR/articles/animations.html): creating, transforming, fading, moving and
  indicating mobjects, composing animations and rate functions.
* [Updaters and value trackers](https://adamrsophie.github.io/manimR/articles/updaters.html): functions that run every
  frame, `ValueTracker` and `always_redraw()`.
* [Text, math and tables](https://adamrsophie.github.io/manimR/articles/text-and-math.html): `Text()`, `MarkupText()`,
  LaTeX with `Tex()` and `MathTex()`, Typst, code listings, numbers,
  matrices and tables.
* [Graphs, plots and coordinate systems](https://adamrsophie.github.io/manimR/articles/graphing.html): number lines, axes,
  function plots, areas, network graphs, vector fields and charts.
* [Cameras and 3D scenes](https://adamrsophie.github.io/manimR/articles/cameras-and-3d.html): moving and zooming cameras,
  3D axes, surfaces, solids and camera orientation.
* [Colors, images, SVG and point clouds](https://adamrsophie.github.io/manimR/articles/colors-images.html): the color
  constants and palettes, `ManimColor`, images, SVG files and point clouds.
* [Rendering, configuration and output](https://adamrsophie.github.io/manimR/articles/rendering.html): `render()`,
  qualities, formats, configuration, sections, sound, subcaptions, caching
  and the command line.
* [RStudio, knitr, Quarto and Shiny](https://adamrsophie.github.io/manimR/articles/rstudio-knitr-shiny.html): RStudio
  addins, the `manim` knitr engine and interactive scenes.
* [Math and utility functions](https://adamrsophie.github.io/manimR/articles/utilities.html): Bezier curves, space
  operations, interpolation and the other helper functions.

## Getting help

Every constructor has a help page with its arguments, for example
`?Circle` or `?Axes`, and the reference index on the website groups them by
topic. Because manimR mirrors Python manim, the
[Manim Community documentation](https://docs.manim.community/) and its
example gallery are useful too: most examples run in R after the small
changes described in [Coming from Python manim](https://adamrsophie.github.io/manimR/articles/coming-from-python.html).
